pull.title: KAFKA-21238: Deep-copy consumer assignor input assignments
pull.body:
Consumer assignor inputs share mutable partition sets with the
coordinator's target assignment. A custom assignor can modify these
sets, silently changing coordinator state and suppressing target
assignment change records.

Deep-copy assignments in `MemberSubscriptionAndAssignmentImpl` and make
the nested sets immutable. Add regression tests for immutability and
isolation from source mutations, and update two reassignment tests to
accept equivalent valid assignments regardless of iteration order.

Similar issue in KS also had been resolved by
https://github.com/apache/kafka/pull/22970.

Reviewers: David Jacot <dajac@apache.org>

repo.name: kafka
repo.description: Apache Kafka - A distributed event streaming platform

reviews.body: @chickenchickenlove Thanks for the update and sorry for the delay. I left a few more comments.

Thanks for the patch!

The new tests have an AI-tooling vibe which I am not a fan of - AI written tests tend to disregard existing conventions (naming, structure), overlap in coverage and spam asserts without much thought behind it.

review_comments.diff_hunk:
@@ -85,7 +90,7 @@ public static Assignment fromRecord(
         return new Assignment(
             record.topicPartitions().stream().collect(Collectors.toMap(
                 ConsumerGroupTargetAssignmentMemberValue.TopicPartition::topicId,
-                topicPartitions -> new HashSet<>(topicPartitions.partitions())))
+                topicPartitions -> Set.copyOf(topicPartitions.partitions())))
review_comments.body: We copy here and then re-copy in the Assignment constructor. We should try to void it.

We need to review how we use Assignment because we may have undesired copies with this change. In general, I wonder if should make the constructor private and have helper with explicit copy or not. e.g. Assignment.copyOf, Assignment.of, etc. Would it help?

@dajac 
Thanks for your comments! 
It helps me a lot.  🙇‍♂️ 
You are right. I've created new commit to address it. 

I've made the constructor private and introduced `Assignment.of()` and `Assignment.copyOf()` to make the copying behavior explicit. I've also removed the redundant copying in `fromRecord()`.

When processing the `assignor`'s output, we check whether it returned the same map instance that was provided as input. If so, we use `Assignment.of()` to reuse the existing immutable data. Otherwise, we use `Assignment.copyOf()` because the returned map and its partition sets may be mutable.

What do you think?
On the output side, we know that we won't touch it so I am inclined to not ensuring the immutability in order to save the cost of doing it.

Ah, that makes sense. You're right.  🙇‍♂️ 

Even if the assignor returns a mutable assignment, replay reconstructs an immutable assignment from the target assignment records. Subsequent assignor calls use this replayed state, and the coordinator only reads the assignor's output, so we don't need a defensive copy in `TargetAssignmentBuilder`.

I've addressed it.
A defensive copy does not seem necessary here because we create the assignment here. Should we rather ensure that `assignedPartitions` is immutable when created and then transfer the ownership?
nit: Let's revert this one.
I think that this code is gone in trunk but, if not, we should use `Assignment.EMPTY`.
Why do we need this change? It seems unrelated.
Do we really need this? Could we just look up the target assignment after the replay?
It seems that this is slightly less efficient than `unmodifiableSet(new HashSet())`.

Are we trying to guard against
1) a badly written custom assignor updating the sets after it has returned them, or
2) coordinator code reaching into the assignment and updating the `Set<Integer>`? 

The reasoning works for 2) but not for 1). When assignor offload is enabled, the record-building step can be delayed until after another group invokes the custom assignor.

We've lost the `AssignorHelpers.isImmutableMap` assert which is the particular behavior that the existing uniform assignors depend upon. The write operations throwing does not imply that `AssignorHelpers.isImmutableMap` will return `true`. `Map.copyOf` return values are immutable but aren't counted by `AssignorHelpers.isImmutableMap` for example.

nit: This assert seems trivially true? We would have to really mess up the implementation of `clear()` and `remove()` above somehow to break it.
```suggestion
```
nit: There's a lot of overhead in these tests just for one line of actual interesting setup. We could combine the two.

We don't assert equality in the `copyOf` immutability test, where it is arguably more likely to break.
Shall we add equality tests to `copyOf`?
These assertions don't test a property of `of` method but rather the input maps and sets.

We've already tested this in the immutability tests above.
```suggestion
```
Do we really need to test this? It's incredibly unlikely we'd ever reach into a record and modify its collections in place. They're also `List`s instead of `Set`s.
It is inconsistent that the new tests use this helper method and the others do not.
Isn't this fully implied by the next test?
Do we really need the `unmodifiableMap` case?
nit: Could we move this up just after `testAssignment` and call it `testAssignmentWithMissingMemberAssignment` or something like that?
Thanks for pointing this out, agreed!

This test change was introduced in an earlier commit because defensively copying the assignment changed its iteration order. That copy has since been removed, so this change is no longer necessary. I overlooked reverting it in the subsequent commits. I'll restore the original test inputs and assertions.

I will remove them in the next commit.
I've moved this test code to `testOfWrapsMapAndReusesPartitionSets()` which will be introduced in the next commit!

My Fault, agreed..! (Sorry for the inconvenience)
I've reverted it in the next commit
Let me check the assignment offloading path first!

@squah-confluent @dajac 

Thanks for pointing out the offloading case. I agree that `Assignment.copyOf()` would protect against subsequent mutations after the copy completes. I was wondering how far we would like to extend that protection in this change. (AFAIK, Assignment Offloading hasn't been integrated yet, so I'm responding based on my understanding of how it might conceptually be applied in `maybeUpdateTargetAssignment()`. 😅 )

With assignment offloading, another `assign()` invocation on the same assignor may run before records are built from the previous result. If invocations run concurrently, the original maps or sets could also be modified while `Assignment.copyOf()` is copying them. Protecting against that case would require copying and mutations to coordinate through the same synchronization mechanism.

My understanding is that case (1) arises when an assignor retains references to objects it has returned and reuses or modifies them in subsequent invocations. If we require assignors not to modify returned maps or sets after returning them, `Assignment.of()` should be sufficient here. Otherwise, `Assignment.copyOf()` would provide additional protection, although it comes with a copying cost and does not fully address concurrent mutations during copying.

Separately, I think assignments reconstructed during replay still need to be immutable. This prevents an assignor from modifying the coordinator’s in-memory state through its inputs without corresponding records.

Would it make sense to clarify whether this change should focus on protecting replayed state from mutation through assignor inputs, or also provide protection against assignors modifying their outputs after returning them?

Please share your thoughts 🙇‍♂️

issue_comments.body: This seems pretty expensive with large groups. Any idea of the cost? Have you considered making them immutable at the source (e.g. when the assignment are created)? The members are immutable in the group so we should start there.

@dajac 
Thanks for the comments!  🙇‍♂️ 

I’ve moved the defensive copy into the Assignment constructor so that assignments are immutable when created, and `MemberSubscriptionAndAssignmentImpl` now reuses them directly.

As you mentioned, the additional copying could be expensive for large consumer groups. How about first using JFR to compare the previous approach with immutability enforced at assignment creation, varying the number of members, topics, and partitions to assess allocation overhead and processing time?

If the overhead is still substantial, another option would be to document the read-only contract clearly in the assignor interfaces and require implementations to copy assignments before modifying them. That would avoid defensive copying, but would leave coordinator state vulnerable to accidental input mutation.

What do you think?

@chickenchickenlove Running benchmarks is always a good idea so I agree with you. I also agree that we must ensure that the input to the assignor is immutable. However, we should do it in a way which avoid copying on every call to the assignor.
Because CI was failed, I rebased onto abc2906503.

timeline.body: This seems pretty expensive with large groups. Any idea of the cost? Have you considered making them immutable at the source (e.g. when the assignment are created)? The members are immutable in the group so we should start there.

@dajac 
Thanks for the comments!  🙇‍♂️ 

I’ve moved the defensive copy into the Assignment constructor so that assignments are immutable when created, and `MemberSubscriptionAndAssignmentImpl` now reuses them directly.

As you mentioned, the additional copying could be expensive for large consumer groups. How about first using JFR to compare the previous approach with immutability enforced at assignment creation, varying the number of members, topics, and partitions to assess allocation overhead and processing time?

If the overhead is still substantial, another option would be to document the read-only contract clearly in the assignor interfaces and require implementations to copy assignments before modifying them. That would avoid defensive copying, but would leave coordinator state vulnerable to accidental input mutation.

What do you think?

@chickenchickenlove Running benchmarks is always a good idea so I agree with you. I also agree that we must ensure that the input to the assignor is immutable. However, we should do it in a way which avoid copying on every call to the assignor.
